newsitem.title: GERMANY: German monetary policy on the turn in '98.
newsitem.headline: German monetary policy on the turn in '98.

text.p: Key German interest rates will remain steady for the rest of 1997, but monetary conditions will begin to tighten at the turn of the year, a Reuters survey of economists showed on Wednesday.

While M3 money supply growth, which the Bundesbank says is one of its main indicators, is set to decline over the coming months, it will not reach the central bank's target zone of 3.5 to 6.5 percent until the second half of the year.
Economists said this slowdown in money circulation, coupled with a calm inflation scene and a patchy economic recovery, would prevent any tightening of rates for the time being.
But most also said the M3 easing would not be enough to prompt a similar easing in credit.
The survey, of 27 economists based in Germany, gave an average forecast of 2.52 percent for the Bundesbank's discount rate by the fourth quarter of 1997, and 4.53 percent for the lombard rate.
In the initial three months of 1998, the rates, currently at 2.50 and 4.50 percent respectively, will tick up to 2.65 and 4.61, average (mean) forecasts showed.

"We expect economic growth of around 2.5 in both 1997 and 1998, which is not really compatible with interest rates at record lows," said Matthias Haffner, economist at BZW in Frankfurt. "That is why we believe the Bundesbank will very slowly increase interest rates over the course of 1998."

But while the average forecast for monetary policy suggests a stable environment will prevail, some analysts said Bundesbank negligence now will mean stinging rate hikes were on the cards in the future.
Both Merrill Lynch and MM Warburg in Frankfurt said they expected the Bundesbank to have upped its key interest rates by 100 basis points apiece by the end of 1998.
Joerg Kraemer, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt said his relatively bearish predictions for rates were based on a view that Bundesbank is already well behind the curve.
"The Bundesbank should already have hiked interest rates at the end of last year -- mainly due to rising capacity utilisation," he said.

"The pro-EMU Bundesbank wants to keep rates articially low at current levels to avoid tensions within the ERM. But by the end of this year, it will be forced to act. It cannot postpone a rise interest rates for too long."

At the other end of the scale, one bank, the Frankfurter Sparkasse, predicted German rates still had room to come down first, saying the Bundesbank would cut each of its key rates by 50 basis points in the third quarter of this year and keep them that way until the second quarter of 1998.
For bond market players, the survey held little joy, with all except one of those asked predicting two years of steadily falling prices and rising yields.

The yield on the 10-year benchmark Bund trading now at just under 6.0 percent, will climb to around 6.72 percent by the end of next year, already reaching 6.35 percent by the close of 1997, the poll showed.
BZW, one of the more bearish on debt prices, said the benchmark would be yielding 6.8 percent by New Year 1999, while IBJ Deutschland was forecasting a rise to 7.20 percent.
BZW's Haffner said that not only the domestic interest rate environment, but also several external issues, would weigh on German debt prices.

"There are two negative factors in the pipeline," he said. "Our fear is that monetary union (EMU) will not go as smoothly as some people now hope -- driving investors out of core European currency debt -- and we are also afraid of further interest rate increases in the U.S., which will have a negative effect on the German market."
